thread.title: Grass, trash leading cause of code violations in Hot Springs
thread.title_full: Grass, trash leading cause of code violations in Hot Springs

author: @TheSenRec
title: Grass, trash leading cause of code violations in Hot Springs
text:
Nearly 9 in 10 code enforcement cases opened by the city of Hot Springs through August involved property conditions such as overgrown grass, trash, debris or inoperable vehicles — everyday problems city officials say they usually try to resolve before taking a property owner to court.
The city opened 261 code enforcement cases through Aug. 31 and closed 237, according to city data. Of those opened, 234 were classified as premises violations.
Neighborhood Services Manager James Hardage said no single problem dominates those cases, but overgrown yards, trash and debris are among the most common.
"Mostly it's just outside stuff," Hardage said. "So it'll be grass and trash and debris in the yard. Those are the most common things we deal with."
The numbers have remained fairly steady from year to year, he said.
The city also opened 12 housing cases, eight Clean Sweep cases, six vacant structure cases and one abandoned auto case through August.
Hardage said that last number does not show the full picture because inoperable vehicles can now be included in a broader premises case when other violations are also present.
April had the most new cases, with 56, followed by June with 51 and March with 48.
Some problems can be surprisingly seasonal. Hardage said inspectors often see discarded mattresses pile up after major holiday sales.
"People will buy a new mattress, and instead of taking the old mattress to the curb and calling CAPS, they just lean it up against the house or they throw it out in the backyard," he said.
CAPS, or Clean, Attractive Property Service, is a city Solid Waste Department program that collects bulky items such as mattresses, furniture, appliances and large brush.
Hardage said people who recently moved to Hot Springs are sometimes unaware they must schedule CAPS pickup instead of simply leaving large items at the curb.
That is one reason officials said education comes before punishment in most cases.
When inspectors find a violation, either through a complaint or while checking neighborhoods, they first try to speak with the property owner and generally give about seven days to correct the problem. If it remains, the city sends a letter identifying the violation and schedules another inspection.
More warnings and attempts to contact the owner typically follow before a citation is issued.
"We do everything possible to not write a citation," Hardage said. "If they didn't have the money to remove something or repair something, they don't have the money to go to court and pay court fines either."
Planning and Development Director Kathleen Sellman said citations are "very rare."
For routine problems such as tall grass or trash, Hardage said he generally wants cases resolved within 30 to 45 days. More serious housing problems, such as a damaged roof, can take longer.
If repeated warnings fail, the city can issue a citation or correct some violations itself and place the cost as a lien on the property.
Condemnation of unsafe buildings is also a last resort, Sellman said.
"When the city does condemn a structure, that is the absolute last resort," she said. "We have tried everything, picked up every rock, looked everywhere, talked to people in the area, title work. We have gone the whole way."
Sellman said condemnation removes the unsafe structure but does not transfer ownership of the property to the city. The land remains privately owned, a distinction she said is often misunderstood.
The city's next concentrated cleanup effort will run Oct. 6-24 in an area of about 530 addresses between Summer Street and Airport Property, from the railroad tracks south to Emory Street.
During the three-week Operation Clean Sweep, city employees will first distribute information about services and identify possible violations. CAPS crews will collect curbside items the following week, and inspectors will return during the final week to check remaining problems.
The effort is one of three Clean Sweeps the city conducts each year and is designed to give residents both notice of violations and a way to correct them before stronger enforcement becomes necessary.
